chunks.title: Reading the red eye: cytology & signs
chunks.tldr: Scraping tells you the bug class: PMNs = bacterial, mononuclear = viral, mixed PMN + mononuclear (+ plasma cells, Leber cells) = chlamydia, eosinophils = allergic. Papillae: vascular core, nonspecific (bacterial, allergic, CL). Follicles: avascular lymphoid centre with vessels around the edge — viral, chlamydial, drug toxicity. Giant papillae: upper tarsus in VKC/GPC, lower in AKC.
points: Pseudomembrane peels without bleeding; true membrane bleeds when stripped.
Ligneous conjunctivitis = recurrent membranes (plasminogen deficiency).
Granuloma + big preauricular node = Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome.
Preauricular node: prominent in viral, chlamydial, gonococcal; rare in plain bacterial.
chunks.hook: Follicle = blood vessels round the outside; papilla = vessel in the middle.

cards.q: Which conjunctivitis shows a mixed PMN and mononuclear cytology?
cards.a: Chlamydial (trachoma / inclusion conjunctivitis).

cards.q: How to tell a pseudomembrane from a true membrane?
cards.a: Pseudomembrane peels off leaving intact epithelium; a true membrane leaves a raw bleeding surface.

chunks.title: Bacterial conjunctivitis: hyperacute to chronic
chunks.tldr: Hyperacute purulent = Neisseria (gonorrhoeae, meningitidis): copious pus, chemosis, node; can perforate the cornea fast. Rx: ceftriaxone 1 g IM once (cornea involved → 1–2 g IV daily ×5 d) + saline irrigation + treat chlamydia/partners. Acute mucopurulent: S pneumoniae, H aegyptius. Subacute: H influenzae. Chronic: staph blepharoconjunctivitis, Moraxella (angular).
points: Uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis self-limits in 10–14 days; 1–3 days with treatment.
Chronic unilateral 'conjunctivitis' → look for dacryocystitis or canaliculitis (pouting punctum, Actinomyces).
Gram stain + culture for any hyperacute case.
chunks.hook: Pus pouring out overnight = gonococcus until proven otherwise — systemic ceftriaxone.

cards.q: Treatment of adult gonococcal conjunctivitis without corneal involvement?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose, plus irrigation and chlamydia cover; treat partners.

cards.q: Unilateral mucopurulent conjunctivitis that won't settle — what to check?
cards.a: The lacrimal system: dacryocystitis or canaliculitis (Actinomyces).

chunks.title: Trachoma
chunks.tldr: C trachomatis serovars A–C, spread by eye-to-eye/flies in poor hygiene. Follicles on upper tarsus → scarring (Arlt line), Herbert's pits (necrosed limbal follicles), superior pannus, then entropion/trichiasis → corneal opacity: leading infectious cause of blindness. Rx: azithromycin 1 g single dose (mass treatment) or doxycycline 100 mg bd ×3 wk; no tetracyclines under 7 y or in pregnancy. Trichiasis → lid surgery.
points: WHO SAFE: Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement.
Herbert's pits are pathognomonic of past trachoma.
chunks.hook: A–C trachoma = Africa/Asia Child blinding; D–K = genital inclusion.

cards.q: What are Herbert's pits?
cards.a: Small depressions at the superior limbus from necrosed limbal follicles — a sign of trachoma.

cards.q: Mass treatment drug for trachoma?
cards.a: Single-dose oral azithromycin 1 g (20 mg/kg in children).

chunks.title: Inclusion conjunctivitis (adult & neonatal)
chunks.tldr: Serovars D–K, sexually transmitted (≈1 in 300 genital infections reach the eye). Adult: unilateral/bilateral follicular conjunctivitis, tender node, micropannus; lasts 3–9 months untreated. Rx: azithromycin 1 g once or doxycycline 100 mg bd ×7 d + treat partners, screen for other STIs. Newborns (no lymphoid tissue yet) get a papillary, often membranous picture: erythromycin 50 mg/kg/d ×14 d (also treats chlamydial pneumonia).
points: LGV serovars L1–L3 → granulomatous conjunctivitis with huge nodes (Parinaud).
chunks.hook: Chronic follicular conjunctivitis in a young adult = ask about sex.

cards.q: Why is neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis papillary rather than follicular?
cards.a: The newborn conjunctiva has no adenoid (lymphoid) layer until ~2–3 months.

chunks.title: Adenovirus: PCF vs EKC
chunks.tldr: Pharyngoconjunctival fever (adenovirus 3, 4, 7): fever, sore throat, follicular conjunctivitis, non-tender node; kids, swimming pools; ~10 days. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (8, 19, 29, 37): tender node, then subepithelial opacities (immune) after ~2 weeks that blur vision for months; very contagious — nosocomial spread via tonometers/hands.
points: Treatment supportive: cold compresses, tears; peel membranes.
Avoid steroids routinely — they prolong viral shedding and rebound; reserve for disabling SEIs.
Clean instruments; patient off work while eyes are red.

cards.q: Adenovirus types causing EKC?
What causes the late blurring in EKC?
cards.a: Subepithelial corneal infiltrates (immune response to viral antigen).

chunks.title: HSV, zoster, AHC & other viruses
chunks.tldr: HSV conjunctivitis: unilateral follicular, vesicles on lid, maybe dendrites; multinucleated giant cells. Rx: topical trifluridine/ganciclovir gel or oral acyclovir 400 mg 5×/day; neonates → IV acyclovir. Steroids contraindicated. Zoster ophthalmicus: oral acyclovir 800 mg 5×/d, famciclovir 500 mg tds or valacyclovir 1 g tds ×7 d, ideally within 72 h. Acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis: enterovirus 70 / coxsackie A24, explosive epidemics, subconjunctival haemorrhages, 5–7 d.
points: Molluscum nodule on lid margin → chronic follicular conjunctivitis; cure = excise/curette the lesion.
Newcastle disease (poultry workers), measles (Koplik spots on caruncle) also cause conjunctivitis.
chunks.hook: Follicular red eye that won't go → look at the lid margin for a molluscum.

cards.q: Oral acyclovir dose for herpes zoster ophthalmicus?
cards.a: 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (start within 72 h).

cards.q: Causes of acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Enterovirus 70 and coxsackievirus A24.

chunks.title: Fungal & parasitic conjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Candida: white plaques, immunocompromised; amphotericin B or nystatin. Sporothrix, Rhinosporidium (bleeding polyp; excise), Coccidioides (Parinaud from lung disease) are rare. Parasites: Loa loa (African eye worm under conjunctiva, eosinophilia; diethylcarbamazine), Thelazia (dog worm — pick it out), Ascaris juice = violent toxic 'butcher's conjunctivitis' (irrigate), Trichinella (lemon-yellow chemosis over recti), Taenia (subconjunctival cyst), Phthirus pubis (lice/nits on lashes).
points: Lash lice: remove nits, smother with ointment on lid margins; treat contacts, wash bedding.
Ophthalmomyiasis: fly larvae on the surface — remove mechanically.
chunks.hook: Itchy lid margins with 'dandruff' glued to lashes in an adult → pubic lice.

cards.q: Worm visible crossing under the conjunctiva in a patient from West Africa?
cards.a: Loa loa — treat with diethylcarbamazine (and surgical removal).

chunks.title: Hay fever conjunctivitis & the allergy drug toolbox
chunks.tldr: Itching, tearing, chemosis ('eyes sinking in'), ropy discharge with pollen/dander exposure. Drugs: antihistamines (emedastine, levocabastine), mast cell stabilisers (cromolyn, lodoxamide, nedocromil — slower, prophylactic), dual-action (olopatadine, ketotifen, epinastine, azelastine, bepotastine, alcaftadine), NSAIDs (ketorolac). Cold compresses; oral loratadine helps.
points: OTC vasoconstrictors (naphazoline etc.) → rebound redness and follicular reaction.
Eosinophils hard to find on scrapings in hay fever conjunctivitis.
chunks.hook: Itch is the cardinal symptom of allergy — no itch, rethink.

cards.q: Name two dual-action antihistamine/mast cell stabiliser drops.
cards.a: Olopatadine, ketotifen (also epinastine, azelastine, bepotastine, alcaftadine).

chunks.title: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)
chunks.tldr: Boys, prepubertal, warm climates, lasts 5–10 years, worse in spring/summer. Intense itch + ropy discharge. Cobblestone giant papillae on upper tarsus or limbal gelatinous papillae with Horner–Trantas dots (eosinophil collections), pseudogerontoxon. Shield ulcer (superior oval) can scar. Maxwell-Lyons sign = fibrinous pseudomembrane on upper tarsus.
points: Rx: dual-action drops, cold, air-con; short pulse of steroid for flares only (glaucoma/cataract risk).
Severe: cyclosporine or tacrolimus drops; supratarsal steroid injection ± papilla excision for shield ulcer.
Associated with keratoconus; burns out without scarring.
chunks.hook: Itchy boy in spring with cobblestones under his upper lid = VKC.

cards.q: What are Trantas dots?
cards.a: White limbal collections of eosinophils in active (limbal) vernal keratoconjunctivitis.

cards.q: Steroid-sparing drops for severe VKC?
cards.a: Cyclosporine or tacrolimus.

chunks.title: AKC, GPC & phlyctenulosis
chunks.tldr: Atopic KC: adults with eczema; burning, milky conjunctiva, papillae lower tarsus, conjunctival scarring, corneal vascularisation; associations: atopic (anterior shield/posterior subcapsular) cataract, keratoconus, RD, HSV keratitis, staph. GPC: contact lenses/prostheses (basophil-rich, Jones–Mote) — clean/replace lenses, daily disposables, stop wear. Phlyctenule: type IV reaction to staph (TB in endemic areas); limbal nodule, corneal ones leave a triangular scar with base at limbus; dramatic response to topical steroid.
points: Conjunctival phlyctenules leave no scar; corneal ones always scar.
Contact blepharitis from neomycin/atropine/preservatives → remove the agent.
chunks.hook: VKC = upper lid, boys, spring. AKC = lower lid, adults, eczema, scarring.

cards.q: Commonest cause of phlyctenulosis in developed countries?
cards.a: Delayed hypersensitivity to Staphylococcus aureus antigens (TB in endemic regions).

cards.q: Cataract associated with atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a: Anterior shield-like or posterior subcapsular cataract.

chunks.title: Pemphigoid, SJS/TEN & Sjögren
chunks.tldr: Mucous membrane pemphigoid: elderly, chronic 'resistant conjunctivitis' → fornix shortening, symblepharon, entropion/trichiasis, blindness; biopsy shows linear IgG/IgA/C3 at basement membrane. Rx: dapsone, systemic immunosuppression, biologics. SJS/TEN: drug-triggered, membranous conjunctivitis acutely (~6 wk), then scarring, dry eye, trichiasis — topical steroids may melt cornea. Sjögren: dry eye + dry mouth; anti-Ro/La, lip biopsy.
points: Superior limbic KC: upper limbus/tarsus, rose bengal staining, filaments; ~50% thyroid; silver nitrate, resect conjunctiva.
Reiter (reactive arthritis): urethritis + arthritis + papillary conjunctivitis, HLA-B27.
Kawasaki: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis + fever, rash, cardiac risk.
chunks.hook: Look in the lower fornix — shallow fornix in an old person = pemphigoid.

cards.q: Immunofluorescence finding in mucous membrane pemphigoid?
cards.a: Linear deposition of IgG/IgA/IgM/complement along the epithelial basement membrane.

cards.q: Thyroid association of which conjunctival disease?
cards.a: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (~50%).

chunks.title: Chemical burns, toxic drops & rosacea
chunks.tldr: Alkali saponifies fats and penetrates deep (worse); acid coagulates protein and stays superficial. Irrigate immediately and copiously — no antidotes; remove particles; then intensive steroid, ascorbate & citrate, cycloplegic, IOP control; later amniotic membrane, limbal stem cell transplant. Toxic conjunctivitis from brimonidine, apraclonidine, preservatives: follicular, persists weeks after stopping. Ocular rosacea: lid margin telangiectasia, MGD, inferior wedge pannus/ulcer; Rx lid care + oral doxycycline.
points: Ophthalmia nodosa = caterpillar hairs → granulomas; remove each hair.
Folliculosis/Axenfeld: benign childhood follicles, self-limiting.

cards.q: Why are alkali burns worse than acid?
cards.a: Alkalis saponify cell membrane lipids and penetrate deeply and continue damaging; acids precipitate proteins, forming a barrier.

chunks.title: Pinguecula, pterygium, SCH & ophthalmia neonatorum
chunks.tldr: Pinguecula: yellow nasal interpalpebral nodule (elastotic); pingueculitis → weak steroid/NSAID. Pterygium: fleshy wing onto cornea (UV, dust, wind); excise if growing toward pupil, conjunctival autograft lowers recurrence. Subconjunctival haemorrhage: reassure, clears 1–3 wk; recurrent/bilateral → check clotting. Ophthalmia neonatorum by onset: gonococcal 2–3 d (ceftriaxone 125 mg IM once), HSV 2–3 d (acyclovir 30 mg/kg/d ×14 d, admit), chlamydia 5–12 d (oral erythromycin ×2 wk); treat parents.
points: Crede silver nitrate prevents gonococcal but not chlamydial or HSV; erythromycin/tetracycline ointment alternatives.
Cat-scratch (Bartonella henselae) = commonest Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome.
chunks.hook: Newborn red eye: Day 2–3 Gonococcus/Herpes, Day 5–12 Chlamydia.

cards.q: Treatment of neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM single dose (plus irrigation; treat parents).

cards.q: What surgical step reduces pterygium recurrence?
cards.a: Conjunctival autograft at excision.

chunks.title: Benign & premalignant conjunctival lesions
chunks.tldr: Nevus: childhood onset, limbal, interpalpebral, contains cysts (reassuring). Limbal dermoid: white mass straddling inferotemporal limbus with hairs; bilateral → Goldenhar. Haemangioma/lymphangioma: hard to excise. PAM: acquired flat brown patch in middle-aged/older, unilateral — premalignant if atypia; biopsy, cryo, MMC. Dysplasia/CIN: grey translucent limbal/corneal epithelium; excise or topical MMC, 5-FU, interferon α-2b.
points: Lymphoid hyperplasia & lymphoma: salmon-pink fornix mass — biopsy, low-dose radiotherapy, watch for systemic lymphoma.
chunks.hook: Pigment since childhood with cysts = nevus. New pigment in a 60-year-old = PAM — biopsy.

cards.q: Bilateral limbal dermoids suggest which syndrome?
cards.a: Goldenhar syndrome (oculoauriculovertebral dysplasia).

cards.q: Topical chemotherapy agents for ocular surface neoplasia?
cards.a: Mitomycin C, 5-fluorouracil, interferon alpha-2b.

chunks.title: Malignant conjunctival tumours
chunks.tldr: SCC: limbal interpalpebral, older males (young in xeroderma pigmentosum, HIV); leukoplakic, gelatinous or papillary with feeder vessels. Rx: excision (no-touch) + cryotherapy to margins ± topical MMC/5-FU/IFN. Mucoepidermoid: aggressive yellow variant → often exenteration. Melanoma: from PAM/nevus/de novo; vascular brown nodule; worse if fornix/caruncle, large, recurrent; wide excision + cryo, consider node biopsy. Lymphoma: pink fornix mass, ~20% systemic → radiotherapy. Kaposi: red haemorrhagic nodule in AIDS.
points: Masquerade syndrome: sebaceous carcinoma or CIS posing as chronic conjunctivitis.
chunks.hook: Salmon patch = lymphoma; feeder vessels + white plaque at limbus = SCC.

cards.q: Poor prognostic sites for conjunctival melanoma?
cards.a: Fornix, caruncle (and palpebral) involvement; also thickness and local recurrence.

chunks.title: Tear film & dry eye tests
chunks.tldr: Tear film 7–10 µm: lipid (meibomian, slows evaporation) / aqueous (lacrimal glands; lysozyme, IgA, lactoferrin) / mucin (goblet cells; makes epithelium wettable). Volume ~7 µL, osmolarity ~300 mOsm/L. Tests: Schirmer without anaesthesia <10 mm/5 min abnormal (with anaesthesia <5 mm); TBUT <10 s (normal >15 s, mucin/lipid problem); rose bengal/lissamine green stain devitalised cells; tear osmolarity (most specific); lysozyme/lactoferrin low in Sjögren.
points: Causes: aqueous deficiency (Sjögren, drugs: antihistamines, antimuscarinics, β-blockers), mucin deficiency (vit A, SJS, pemphigoid, trachoma, burns), lipid (blepharitis), exposure.
Earliest sign: thin/absent inferior tear meniscus; interpalpebral staining; filaments.
chunks.hook: Lipid on top, water in the middle, mucus glue at the bottom.

cards.q: Abnormal Schirmer I result (no anaesthesia)?
cards.a: Less than 10 mm wetting in 5 minutes.

cards.q: Which dry eye test is said to be most specific?
cards.a: Tear film hyperosmolarity.

chunks.title: Treating dry eye
chunks.tldr: Chronic — explain it. Ladder: artificial tears (preservative-free if >4×/day; benzalkonium most toxic), gels/ointment at night, Lacrisert, autologous serum, mucolytic acetylcysteine for strands; humidifier, moisture goggles. Anti-inflammatory: cyclosporine 0.05% bd, loteprednol pulses; diquafosol. Treat blepharitis/rosacea (doxycycline), omega-3. Retain tears: punctal plugs → cautery occlusion.
points: Complications of severe dry eye: ulcer, thinning, perforation, infection.

cards.q: Which preservative in eye drops is the most epitheliotoxic?
cards.a: Benzalkonium chloride.
